title: Could This Discovery Help Unlock the Voynich Manuscript's Mysteries?
site_name: ColombiaOne: News from Colombia and the World
excerpt: Could a new discovery reveal how the Voynich Manuscript’s pages were originally arranged, offering clues to its mysteries?
content:
Researchers studying the Voynich manuscript, a 15th-century illustrated book written in an undeciphered script, propose that its pages were originally arranged as individual folded sheets before someone bound them in the wrong order. Their hypothesis could change how scholars study the mysterious text, although it does not explain what the words mean.

The study, Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript, was published in Digital Medievalist. Its authors are Lisa Fagin Davis, executive director of the Medieval Academy of America, and Colin Layfield, an information systems researcher at the University of Malta. They combine physical clues, including illustrations that appear to continue across separated pages, with statistical analysis of the manuscript’s writing.

Their approach uses latent semantic analysis (LSA), a computational technique that compares patterns in text without requiring researchers to understand its language. The results suggest that the manuscript’s original structure differed from the surviving copy, although it remains uncertain how reliably this method can reconstruct the text’s initial sequence.

What the statistical analysis found

Medieval books were commonly assembled from quires: groups of folded sheets nested together and sewn into booklets. Davis and Layfield propose a different original structure for the Voynich manuscript. They suggest it began as individual folded sheets, each forming two leaves, known as singulions, that were not intended to be bound together into conventional quires or a book. Someone later assembled them into the volume that survives today, disrupting their original order.

The researchers applied LSA to text from different pages, leaves, folded sheets and gatherings. They also used known medieval manuscripts as calibration material to help assess how textual patterns could reflect document structure.

LSA maps relationships between words and textual patterns to identify links in undeciphered writing. However, similarity scores alone cannot establish meaning or verify where a page belongs.

The statistical results are only part of the researchers’ argument. The findings also reveal distinct handwriting styles across the manuscript. The current arrangement places pages attributed to different scribes together in ways Davis and Layfield consider inconsistent with typical medieval book production.

The illustrations provide another clue. In several cases, an image appears to reach the edge of one page and continue on another page that now sits much farther away in the volume. If the sheets were originally arranged differently, those separated parts might have belonged together.

The idea that the manuscript’s current order may be wrong is not new. The researchers’ contribution is a more specific hypothesis about its original structure, supported by a combination of textual analysis and physical evidence.

What is known about the manuscript?

The Voynich manuscript is named after Wilfrid Voynich, the antiquarian bookseller who acquired it from a Jesuit collection in Italy in 1912. Today, it resides at Yale University’s Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library (MS 408), which provides public online access to high-resolution scans of its pages.

Radiocarbon dating places the parchment between 1404 and 1438. That range dates the material used to make the manuscript, not necessarily the exact time when its text and illustrations were produced. The author, language and precise place of origin remain unknown.

The illustrations include plants that cannot be confidently identified, astronomical and astrological diagrams, bathing figures and elaborate cosmological drawings. Other pages resemble collections of herbal or pharmaceutical information. These images have inspired theories about the manuscript’s purpose, but no widely accepted interpretation has emerged.

Its early ownership history is also incomplete. In a 1665 letter to the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher, Johannes Marcus Marci reported that Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II had bought the book for 600 gold ducats. Marci’s letter is the source of that account; no independent purchase record confirms the transaction. The manuscript later belonged to the physician and pharmacist Jacobus de Tepenec, whose signature remains faintly visible on an early page, before passing through other owners and eventually reaching Voynich.

What could the hypothesis change?

If the manuscript’s pages are out of order, studies that assume the existing sequence is original may need to be reconsidered. Davis has indicated that the analysis offers clearer hypothetical sequences for quires 13 and 20, while the first eight quires may not have one definitive sequence. The researchers’ work therefore does not establish a complete reconstruction of the book.

The proposed ordering method has also drawn methodological criticism. Voynich researcher Torsten Timm, in a review of the studies, accepts that pages belonging to the same physical folded sheet show elevated textual similarity. However, he questions whether that pattern proves the sheets were intended to follow one another in a particular reading order.

Timm argues that similar vocabulary does not necessarily mean that pages belong next to each other in a meaningful text. His review also raises questions about how the researchers tested their proposed sequences against alternative arrangements. The debate centers on how much the statistical results can establish about the manuscript’s original organization.

Davis and Layfield are considering comparing the shape of a large water stain along the manuscript’s upper margins across different pages. Because the stain does not appear symmetrically where corresponding pages would be expected to align, its patterns could help test possible arrangements and provide further evidence about how the manuscript was assembled.

Davis remains hopeful that decipherment will eventually be possible. In a 2023 lecture at Wellesley College, she said: “I am hopeful that as more computing power is thrown at this, as more interdisciplinary collaborations take place, I think we’ll get there. I really do.”
